What is Roth Cost Basis on a 401k? I used to think the Roth Cost Basis was my Roth principle, ie the money I can take out whenever with no penalty. Comparing my end of 2024 and 2025 statements though the math didn't workout. I put in the $23.5K max as all Roth plus another $8.5K as an automatic After Tax Roth Conversion (MegaBackdoor Roth). My Roth Cost Basis only went up $21.8K though. So what is Roth Cost Basis and how do I find out my Total Roth Contributions for the account? The pic is on my quarterly 401K statement.  Commenting because I'm curious to see the answer.
It must have something to do with the MegaBackdoor Roth because this doesn't show up on any statements prior to me maxing out my 401k for first time in 2023 even though I have been doing all Roth since 2019. 

I put in like $8500 over the limit last year so that doesn't really jive with the $21k increase in basis either.
The basis is what you contributed but not the growth or conversions. You cannot take this out within the 401k without penalty if the value is greater than basis because distributions from a Roth 401k are on a pro rata basis (meaning if half the account is basis and half is gain, drawing any amount will be treated as half gain half basis). This is notably different from a Roth IRA where basis may be drawn out first with no tax or penalty at any age for any reason. The conversion you made via the Megabackdoor provisions is not treated as a contribution for purposes of basis inclusion to avoid the 5 year rule, But may be withdrawn without ordinary tax consequences before 59.5 because tax is paid when converted in plan (even if nullified via a nondeductible traditional contribution converting in plan, in other words: it doesn’t matter if you actually paid tax to convert or converted nondeductible traditional contributions). 

If the question is why is the 8.5k conversion not added to basis, it is because it is not basis, but it is also not taxable as gains for purposes of early withdrawal like normal gains from the account with the exception of the 10% penalty for the first 5 years.

If the question is how much you may withdraw without early withdrawal penalty, it is the sum of the basis and all in plan conversion. Note this would still happen pro rata, triggering tax and penalty on gain If you plan to do that before a rollover to a Roth IRA and achieving age 59.5, because the pro rata rule will kick in. If the pro rata rule kicks in, your tax liability will be (basis + conversion) / total account basis * ordinary income tax rate + 10% penalty.

Apologies if this is still unclear. Conversions in a Roth 401k are a weird pseudo situation that are technically not gain or basis. When explaining this normally, I am doing so to financial professionals with a solid working understanding of these terms and rules. 

Source: CFP tutor.

Vanguard decided to FAFO with their $100 full transfer out fee, so now I'm cancelling my advisor services Let me preface this by saying I know I'm an insignificant fish in their big pool of investors.  They don't care about my fees and won't notice if I drop them.  I'm simply sharing if anyone else is on the fence about Personal Advisor services...

**TL;DR: I'm now of the opinion you're probably better setting up a simple 60% VTI / 30% VXUS / 10% BND automated investing plan and taking 15 minutes a year to rebalance if needed.  The fee for advisor services probably isn't worth it.**

I've been a PA client for nearly 10 years, paying the 0.3% AUM advisory fee which equates to well over $1k a year in fees.

Earlier this month, I had a small lump of cash (no investments) in an unmanaged taxable account that I wanted to move to Fidelity.  Since I planned to close that account anyway, I did a full ACATS transfer and got hit with a $100 "full transfer & closure" fee that I guess the introduced in 2024.  And the kicker is I could have avoided this by just withdrawing the cash via ACH and then transferring it over to Fidelity.

Figuring I've earned some good with being a PA client for all these years, I asked for a fee waiver because I was unaware of the new fee and it was a silly mistake where I could have avoided the fee by withdrawing my money instead of ACATS.

Their answer? No.  They don't offer waivers and they pointed me to their fee schedule.

I explained that the wording of the fee schedule wasn't clear:

>*Vanguard Brokerage may charge a $100 processing fee for each account closure and full transfer of account assets to another firm....The fee will not be assessed for clients who hold at least $5 million in qualifying Vanguard assets or brokerage accounts enrolled in a Vanguard-affiliated advisory service.*

I don't know if that meant ($5M AUM) OR (brokerage accounts enrolled in advisory services) or if it meant $5M in advisory services.  But the fact that it says "may charge" suggests there is a way to waive the fee.  Their answer was still "No".

So then I pointed out I pay over $1k a year in advisory fees.  If they want to nickel and dime me, I can do the same in return.  They had a choice: waive the $100 one-time fee and keep my annual advisor fees, or keep the one-time $100 and loose the $1k+ per year fees I'm paying them.

They chose to keep the $100.  So I'm out.

Funny thing is, when trying to decide if I was overreacting, I did some reflecting on what I was getting out of PA.  The answer was mostly just "$1k less per year in fees".

Here's why:

* My "aggressive" asset mix of 90% stocks, 10% bonds has turned into an 11-fund portfolio under their management.  I did a backtested comparison of that with 60% VTI / 30% VXUS / 10% BND and **the non-managed, 3-fund method comes out on top for the past 5, 15, and 30 year period** no matter if you consider lump sum at the start of the period or DCA over the period.  **That 0.3% AUM fee seems cheap, but it adds up.**
* Tax loss harvesting (TLH) is touted as a benefit of the managed plan, but this is really just tax deferral.  It's sort of like pre-tax 401k contributions.  It doesn't waive the fact that eventually when you cash out, you'll still need to pay taxes on the lower cost basis (higher gains to pay taxes for because you lowered the cost basis through TLH).  And even if you consider the taxes you save, you need to probably have close to a million in under management and contributing 5-10k+ a month to offset the 0.3% fee.
* TLH also becomes pointless if you hold your investments long enough that the bulk of them have long-term gains and no losses.
* And the most convincing for me has been the utter lack of usefulness from the "advisors".  They come across as brand new graduate new-hires (if that) reading from a a script.  One even told me the main reason they're helpful is to discourage people from emotionally selling or deviating from their investment plan during downturns or if you want to buy something like a car, etc.  I guess if that's what you need, it's great for you.  But if you have self discipline, you're paying the fee for nothing.  It took me 3 weeks and 3 scheduled calls with an advisor to get an answer to "does my portfolio rebalance and sell assets if I change from PA to the digital advisor?" -- something they should have written down in whatever handbook they're reading from.  On my last call, the advisor took the last 20 minutes of our 30 minute call to ask ME career advice.  Who's paying who?

Long-winded rant to say I'm out.  And if you're on the fence, you should be too.  Stay at Vanguard if you want.  I probably will.  But don't pay for PA.  Just setup automated contributions and let it ride.  If you tend to be emotional during downturns, have your spouse change your password and not share it with you once the auto-investing is setup (but only do this if you trust your spouse, ha!).

EDIT: Fixed my outdated use of "PAS" to mean "Personal Advisor Services"; Vanguard now calls that "PA" and "PAS" is the 500k+ "Select" tier. Their digital advisor is basically VTI-VXUS-BND-BNDX.

You don't need to pay $1000 a year for VT & chill (or VTI & chilll or VOO & chill, etc.).

The inability to trade tons of stocks or ETFs (even Vanguard ETFs!) during 4-5:30pm extended hours and being locked out of trading between 5:30pm-9:00am is my biggest pet peeve. 

I get that they are targeting buy & hold investors but for that small portion of my portfolio I leave for fun, I should be able to make moves when I want to.
There are people who don’t know the difference between a stock and a bond, or are not comfortable investing their money.  They can and likely will) do far worse than Vanguard’s Personal Advisory Service at 0.3% a year.
That's fair.  I guess the realization I came to was that I thought the advisor piece would give me more than just a human walking me through how to setup a robo advisor.  Investing is (usually) better than not investing for most people, so some may find value.  But I'd encourage those who think they need this to also see if can learn how to setup auto investment into 3 funds and save the years of fees.
